title: Topology from Decoherence
authors: Alexandre Chaduteau, Derek Lee, Frank Schindler, Abhinav Prem
abstract: Decoherence is conventionally regarded as an obstacle to realizing topological quantum phases. This has motivated extensive efforts to suppress noise in candidate topological materials and devices. Here, we show that decoherence can instead induce topological phenomena. We demonstrate this in a lattice system subject to environment-induced dephasing. The noise-averaged dynamics, governed by an interacting quantum master equation, realize a topological phase characterized by a winding number and the non-Hermitian skin effect. The dynamical consequence is striking: the correlated nature of the stochastic noise yields asymmetric diffusion, whose direction is fixed by the winding number and is reversible only through a topological phase transition. This effect is induced purely by interactions, distinguishing it from previous studies of free, effectively single-particle systems. It also disappears upon postselecting measurement outcomes, confirming that it is a genuinely open-system phenomenon with no effective Hamiltonian description. Remarkably, the model remains analytically tractable. Our results establish correlated quantum noise as a route to topology in open many-body systems, beyond free-particle and non-Hermitian Hamiltonian paradigms.
summary: The authors demonstrate that decoherence, usually viewed as detrimental, can actually induce robust topological phases in interacting many-body systems. By analyzing the evolution of correlation matrices under a Lindblad master equation, they show that the noise generates spectral features like point gaps and winding numbers. This leads to observable physical consequences, such as asymmetric diffusion whose direction is dictated by the system's topology.
main_problem: To investigate whether decoherence, conventionally seen as an obstacle to topology, can instead induce topological phenomena in interacting many-body systems.
main_result: The noise-averaged dynamics realize a topological phase characterized by a winding number and the non-Hermitian skin effect. This is manifested dynamically through asymmetric diffusion fixed by the system's interactions.
method: Analysis involves solving the equation of motion for two-particle correlation matrices derived from the Lindblad master equation, utilizing momentum-space representations and spectral analysis (winding numbers).
model_or_system: The model is a 1D lattice system of spinless fermions whose time evolution is governed by a Lindblad equation incorporating both coherent Hamiltonian dynamics and environment-induced dephasing jumps. The complexity arises from the interaction terms in the noise operators.
key_observables:
Asymmetric diffusion, winding number ($
u$), non-Hermitian skin effect, and the spectrum of the superoperator $\hat{C}$.
important_parameters: Interaction strength (related to $B$ parameter), lattice hopping ($t$), and system size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on tracking correlation matrices via a linear evolution equation in the superoperator space, requiring various truncations of the infinite-dimensional problem.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spectral structure (point gaps) in both single-particle and two-particle sectors, demonstrating how non-zero winding numbers guarantee boundary modes (skin effect) and asymmetric diffusion in time evolution.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general framework using the Lindblad equation for correlation matrices to analyzing symmetries and spectral properties in momentum space. It then details how breaking inversion symmetry opens a point gap, leading to the prediction of skin effects and finally demonstrating the resulting asymmetric diffusion in long-time dynamics.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete theoretical mechanism showing that non-Hermitian physics and topological invariants can emerge purely from open system dynamics (stochastic noise) rather than being imposed by an effective Hamiltonian, which is highly relevant for understanding realistic quantum devices subject to dissipation.
